name: Hexagonal water

lead: Hexagonal water is a wellness term for water said to be arranged in six-sided molecular clusters. Promoters say it hydrates cells more efficiently, supports nutrient uptake and helps skin look clearer and more hydrated.

Published chemistry describes hexagonal structure in ice, not in drinking water: hydrogen bonds in liquid water form and break in under a picosecond. Encyclopedic sources classify the drinking-water claims as pseudoscience, and no human trials on skin appearance are known.

paras: People buy bottled or filtered "hexagonal" water, or devices and additives that claim to restructure it, and drink it as a hydration routine. Some use it in skincare-adjacent wellness regimens.

The water itself is ordinary water, so direct health risk is low; the main cost is price for products and devices. Regulators and critics have described structured-water marketing claims as unsupported.

chain: Skin looks more hydrated and clear
angle.text: Proponents drink hexagonal water as part of a hydration routine in the belief that it improves skin appearance. The proposed chain is claimed by sellers and has not been tested in trials.

lead: Hexagonal water, also called structured, cluster or gel water, is a wellness concept in which drinking water is said to be arranged into hexagonal molecular rings. Promoters claim this improves hydration, nutrient absorption and waste removal, and some tie it to better-looking skin.[1]

The term borrows from real chemistry: ordinary ice has a hexagonal crystal lattice, and recent atomic-force microscopy and computational work study its surface and structure.[2][3] Those studies concern ice, not drinking water.

A Wikipedia summary reports that water clusters have been observed but that their hydrogen bonds break and re-form within about 200 femtoseconds, and that NMR comparisons found no significant difference between "hexagonal" and ordinary ultrapure water.[1]

paras: Sellers describe a stable hexagonal arrangement of molecules that the body can absorb more readily, with benefits such as cellular communication and detoxification.[1] Some add that infrared exposure creates the structure; the Wikipedia summary says no scientific evidence supports that.[1]

Physical chemistry research on hexagonal arrangements focuses on ice. A 2024 Nature study imaged the surface of hexagonal ice Ih at atomic resolution, and a 2025 study modelled large hexagonal clusters as a model for ice.[2][3] Reviews of structured-water claims note short lifetimes of clusters in liquid water.[1]
No studies found. Hexagonal-water research in the literature concerns ice and water physics, not skin or hydration outcomes in people.
